title: The Word as Radiance and Substance
english: Preface to Hebrews: The heretics say that this letter is not Paul’s. Their first proof is that his name is not placed at the head of it, as it is in his other letters. Their second is that its style is different, that is, foreign to Paul’s, and so is the way it is put together. We must understand, then, that Paul was hated by the Jews as a man who taught people to abandon the law (Acts 21:21). That is why he was in danger in Jerusalem, barely escaped, and was sent to Rome. So when he wrote something for the good of the Hebrews, he did not put his name at the head of it, so that their hatred of him would not rob them of the benefit of the letter. As the blessed Severian says, he wrote to them in the Hebrew language, and his words were translated by one of his disciples, by Luke, or more likely by Clement, whom he also mentions. That is why the style is foreign. Those before us also looked into this question. Eusebius, the disciple of Pamphilus, who was more of a historian than anyone before or after him, recorded the inquiry, and recorded too that our fathers, the bishops of old, held the letter to be Paul’s.

On Hebrews 1:1–2: “In many parts” refers to the different times in which God arranged our affairs: at the creation of Adam, in the time of Cain, in the time of Noah, in the time of Abraham, before the law and after the law. God’s governance on our behalf has many parts. “In many ways”, because one commandment was given to Adam, another to Noah, another to Abraham, another through Moses, and various commandments through the prophets. “He spoke to us in a Son” stands for “through a Son”: not in him as in an instrument, but through him as the one who carried out his saving work in the flesh. In this way the Jews could begin to listen from there, grasp the Word as if by touch, and so be led up to his existence before the ages. For having first said, “He spoke to us in a Son, whom he also appointed heir” (“appointed” stands for “made”), he raised his discourse to the Son’s existence before the ages. He does this all the time: now he rises to speak of Christ as God, now he comes down to his becoming man.

On Hebrews 1:3: He wanted to show more clearly that the Word was begotten from the Father’s essence, so he spoke of radiance. Radiance comes from the essence of that whose radiance it is; it is continuous with it, it comes from it, and it can never be thought of apart from it. But radiance suggests a nature lesser than that whose radiance it is, and one with no subsistence of its own. So he expressed the point with a second word, saying, “and the exact stamp of his subsistence”. The first word he set down to prove that the Son is from the Father’s essence without division; the second, to show that he is not without a subsistence of his own. Just as John named him “Word” and then added, “he was with God, and he was God” (John 1:1), so Paul said “radiance” and then added, “and the exact stamp of his subsistence”.
On Hebrews 1:3: This is what Jeremiah says: “Mighty are the works of his words” (Joel 2:11).

On Hebrews 1:3: Even though the Word became flesh (John 1:14), he remained in the glory and nature of the Godhead and never left the highest thrones of God the Father. And although he was “made a little lower than the angels” (Hebrews 2:9) because of the measure of humanity …
